paragraphs: An activation rule determines which signals a neural network passes forward. Simple thresholds can make those signals sparse, but they do not explicitly determine whether a feature channel helps the final decision. This paper addresses the resulting interference from irrelevant channels by assessing relevance from two complementary perspectives: a channel’s own activity and its learned contribution to decisions.

The proposed AIEC mechanism combines a basic threshold activation with three units. An Activation-Counting Unit tracks channel activity statistics, while a Decision-Making Unit learns decision weights for channels. A Consensus Gatekeeping Unit then uses agreement between these internal and decision-related assessments to suppress irrelevant channels during training. The central idea is to make suppression depend on evidence of relevance, rather than activity magnitude alone.

Experiments report that AIEC suppresses irrelevant channels, produces sparser representations, and improves performance over existing activation mechanisms across multiple tasks and domains. Its compatibility with several mainstream network architectures suggests that relevance-aware activation can serve as a broadly applicable network component.
icml-2026-activation-with-intrinsic-extr.tldr: AIEC suppresses irrelevant neural-network channels by combining evidence from their activation statistics and learned decision weights.

paragraphs: Estimating probabilities from incomplete information requires both useful explanatory factors and a reliable way to combine them. Existing approaches ask language models to propose factors and rough probabilities, then refine these with Naïve Bayes. Too few factors leave cases unresolved, but simply adding more introduces noise and correlations that undermine the independence assumptions behind that refinement.

ANCHOR organizes explanatory factors into a hierarchy through repeated generation and clustering. It matches a context to this hierarchy using retrieval and refinement, allowing probability inference to draw on a denser, structured factor space. It also supplements Naïve Bayes with a Causal Bayesian Network that represents otherwise hidden dependencies between factors. Together, these components address both missing coverage and unreliable combinations of correlated evidence.

The reported experiments show fewer unknown predictions and more reliable probability estimates than direct language-model baselines. ANCHOR also achieves leading performance while reducing time and token overhead. These findings support hierarchical organization and explicit dependency modeling as complementary ways to improve probability inference.
icml-2026-anchor-abductive-network-const.tldr: ANCHOR organizes explanatory factors hierarchically and models their dependencies to improve language-model-based probability estimates.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns behavior from a fixed dataset. Conservative learning rules help control errors on unfamiliar behavior, but can also preserve the dataset’s biases. Generating extra trajectories offers a way to broaden that experience. The paper argues that existing augmentation methods mostly make local variations while leaving separate behavior patterns disconnected at the level of complete trajectories.

BiTrajDiff constructs trajectories around shared intermediate states called anchors. One diffusion process generates a possible future from an anchor, while another independently generates a history leading into it. Joining these segments at the shared state can create connections between behavior patterns that the original dataset never linked. This changes the structure of the available experience, rather than only adding nearby variants of existing trajectories.

Across the evaluated offline reinforcement-learning backbones, BiTrajDiff consistently outperforms advanced data-augmentation methods. The results support its central proposition: augmentation can be more useful when it recovers connections between behaviors, giving a learner access to coherent combinations absent from its recorded experience.
icml-2026-bitrajdiff-bidirectional-traje.tldr: BiTrajDiff joins independently generated past and future trajectory segments at shared states to connect behaviors missing from offline training data.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time series becomes difficult when observations arrive at uneven intervals and different variables are measured at different times. These conditions disrupt methods built around regularly spaced samples. They also complicate the combination of local changes with longer periodic patterns, because conventional frequency analysis does not directly fit irregular timestamps.

TFMixer addresses both views of the data. Its Global Frequency Module uses a learnable Non-Uniform Discrete Fourier Transform to extract frequency representations directly from irregular observations. In parallel, a Local Time Module uses query-based attention over patches to gather informative temporal segments and reduce the imbalance between densely and sparsely observed regions. The model combines these representations for forecasting and uses an inverse transform to explicitly extend seasonal patterns.

Experiments on real-world irregular time-series benchmarks show effective forecasting and robustness under irregular sampling and missing data. The approach matters because it gives local temporal evidence and global periodic structure distinct modeling mechanisms, while bringing them together in a single forecasting framework.
icml-2026-bridging-time-and-frequency-a-.tldr: TFMixer combines timestamp-aware frequency analysis with local temporal attention to forecast irregularly sampled multivariate time series.

paragraphs: Some image-protection methods add carefully designed perturbations that interfere with a generative model’s ability to learn an image’s underlying content or style. These methods aim to obstruct unauthorized imitation and replication. This paper investigates their robustness by examining what happens when protected images undergo DDIM inversion and reconstruction.

The analysis finds that DDIM inversion amplifies protective perturbations, producing pronounced structural distortions in reconstructed images. The authors turn that response into a signal for purification. Their method, DIRP, minimizes the error between an image and its DDIM-based reconstruction while imposing perceptual constraints. The reconstruction objective targets the disruptive perturbations, and the perceptual constraints help preserve the image’s visible content.

Experiments cover six mimicry-protection methods and compare DIRP with five leading attack baselines. DIRP consistently achieves better perturbation removal while preserving image quality more effectively. These findings expose vulnerabilities in the evaluated protections: a transformation that magnifies their effects can also provide an objective for removing them, motivating stronger protection designs.
icml-2026-ddim-inversion-as-a-perturbati.tldr: DIRP uses DDIM reconstruction errors to remove image-protection perturbations, exposing weaknesses in six evaluated mimicry defenses.

paragraphs: Robot co-design connects choices about a robot’s physical form with choices about how it learns to move. Debate2Create makes that joint search an iterative conversation between language-model agents, grounded in physics-based evaluation. A design agent and a control agent propose, challenge, and reconcile ideas, while judges focused on different criteria provide feedback across multiple objectives.

The debate structure creates repeated opportunities to revise morphology and reward design together. Simulation supplies the physical evaluation that anchors these exchanges. The study uses a fixed-topology protocol with reinforcement learning performed for each candidate, so its findings concern coordinated changes within that particular design and evaluation setup.

Across five MuJoCo locomotion benchmarks, Debate2Create achieves the highest default-normalized score among evaluated language-model and black-box baselines. Reported gains reach 3.2 times on Ant and nearly nine times on Swimmer. Debate improves results by 18–35% over compute-matched zero-shot generation, and generated rewards transfer to default morphologies in four of five tasks. These results suggest that structured interaction contributes useful refinement under the tested protocol.
icml-2026-debate2create-robot-co-design-.tldr: Debate2Create uses simulator-grounded debate between design and control agents to improve joint robot morphology and reward design.

paragraphs: Biomolecular design must coordinate related properties such as sequence and three-dimensional structure. Generative co-design methods model these properties together, but often advance their separate generation processes in parallel with a fixed synchronization. This paper identifies the timing of that coordination as an important design choice that deserves explicit optimization.

The authors argue that an unsuitable temporal relationship between processes can create noisy training supervision and intermediate states that do not agree across modalities. GeoCoupling learns how to coordinate the progression of these heterogeneous processes during training and generation. Its focus is therefore on when different aspects of a molecule develop relative to one another, as well as on modeling those aspects themselves.

Evaluations cover structure-based drug design and unconditional protein design. In these experiments, learned temporal couplings consistently outperform both synchronous and randomly coupled baselines, improving physical validity and diversity. The findings suggest that the schedule connecting generative processes can materially affect molecular quality, making temporal coordination a useful component of biomolecular co-design.
icml-2026-demystifying-multimodal-biomol.tldr: GeoCoupling learns the timing between coupled biomolecular generation processes, improving physical validity and diversity in the evaluated design tasks.

paragraphs: Concept Embedding Models support interpretable prediction by representing meaningful concepts through learned embeddings. The paper identifies a limitation in existing models: treating concepts as independent overlooks relationships among them. When concepts depend on one another, a model needs to represent their joint behavior as well as the distribution of each individual concept.

EC-CEM addresses this through a combination of copula theory and evidential deep learning. A copula separates the distributions of individual concepts from the structure describing their dependencies. This lets the proposed model build a joint concept distribution without forcing those two modeling choices into the same form. The framework also introduces two training objectives that jointly pursue accurate classification and useful concept modeling.

The authors justify the approach through variational inference and report empirical superiority in extensive experiments. The contribution is a way to incorporate concept relationships into an interpretable prediction framework. It addresses the independence assumption directly while retaining flexibility in how individual concepts and their dependencies are represented.
icml-2026-evidential-copula-concept-embe.tldr: EC-CEM combines copulas and evidential learning to model dependencies between interpretable concepts while keeping their individual distributions flexible.

paragraphs: Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms rely on search operators that propose changes to candidate solutions. These operators are often designed by experts, although language models increasingly help automate their construction. This paper argues that optimizing each operator separately misses an important source of performance: the changing relationships between operators used within the same search.

E2OC treats multi-operator optimization as a Markov decision process, framing design as a sequence of choices whose effects depend on the current configuration. It evolves both design strategies and executable code. Monte Carlo Tree Search explores combinations of operator-design strategies, while an operator rotation mechanism helps identify effective configurations. The framework can incorporate established automated heuristic-design methods as the underlying designer.

Experiments span heuristic-design tasks with different objectives and problem scales. E2OC consistently outperforms leading automated-design methods and other frameworks for jointly designing multiple heuristics. The reported generalization and sustained optimization results support designing operators as an interacting collection, with attention to how their combinations perform over successive decisions.
icml-2026-evolving-interdependent-operat.tldr: E2OC improves automated heuristic design by jointly evolving interacting search operators through sequential exploration of their combinations.

paragraphs: Graphical-interface agents often ask a language model to interpret each screen and select the next action from scratch. Repeating that process over a long task can be fragile and expensive. Executable Agentic Memory stores interface knowledge in a structured graph, allowing planning to retrieve and execute known action sequences.

The memory-building pipeline explores interfaces with state-aware depth-first search and mines groups of actions to compress multi-step routines. During planning, a lightweight Q-function estimates the value of choices and guides Monte Carlo Tree Search over the graph. The paper also establishes a bias-consistency result for that value model and derives bounds on the samples needed to recover paths.

On AndroidWorld, EAM reports improvements of up to 19.6% over leading baselines such as UI-TARS-7B. Token costs are reduced sixfold relative to GPT-4o, with average latency of 2.8 seconds. These results show how executable memory can improve both task performance and interaction efficiency by making reusable routines a central part of planning.
icml-2026-executable-agentic-memory-for-.tldr: EAM turns interface experience into an executable knowledge graph, improving GUI-agent performance while reducing token costs.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference uses simulated relationships between parameters and observations to estimate which parameter values are plausible given observed data. Generative models offer a route to efficient posterior estimation, but the paper argues that simply merging heterogeneous inputs loses important differences between parameters and observations. FUSE addresses how these inputs interact and how posterior samples are generated.

Its dual-track architecture maintains distinct representations for the different input types while allowing them to exchange information dynamically. During sampling, a Feynman-Kac steering strategy uses intermediate observation likelihoods to guide generative trajectories. This introduces observation-based guidance along the generation process, helping improve sample quality rather than relying only on the model’s initial conditioning.

On standard simulation-based inference benchmarks, FUSE outperforms leading baselines and produces posterior distributions closely matching reference MCMC results. In an exoplanet orbital-estimation task, it also resolves complex parameter degeneracies that challenge existing methods. These findings indicate potential for scientific problems where multiple parameter combinations can explain similar observations.
icml-2026-fuse-fk-steered-multi-modal-fl.tldr: FUSE combines distinct input-processing tracks with likelihood-guided generation to improve simulation-based posterior estimation.

paragraphs: GoodDiffusion addresses copyright protection by making authorization part of how a diffusion bridge model generates outputs. The aim is to control unauthorized use when it happens. The paper contrasts this approach with watermarking and fingerprinting, which support attribution after use, and defenses that primarily reduce output quality.

The proposed mechanism draws inspiration from backdoors: a signature carried by an input determines whether generation is permitted. Queries with valid signatures retain high-quality generation, while unauthorized inputs are refused. This makes selective access a behavior built into the model’s generative process.

A central finding concerns the weakness of using a fixed signature. The authors empirically show that gradient-based optimization can efficiently recover a substitute signature in naive static-signature designs. Such a substitute undermines authorization because it can provide an alternative way to activate generation.

GoodDiffusion therefore introduces a Learnable Signature Network that produces signatures specific to each input. By removing the shared signature across inputs, this design prevents a recovered substitute from transferring between them. The reported experiments show effective blocking of unauthorized use alongside strong generation quality for authorized users. Together, these findings support input-dependent signatures as a way to strengthen access control while preserving useful generation for permitted queries.
icml-2026-gooddiffusion-proactive-copyri.tldr: GoodDiffusion builds authorization into diffusion bridge models using input-specific signatures, with experiments showing effective blocking of unauthorized use while preserving authorized generation quality.

paragraphs: Generating several reasoning paths can improve language-model accuracy, but the available computation must be divided between exploring alternatives and refining promising ones. HyPER builds on two observations: the useful balance changes during reasoning, and correct and incorrect paths often separate only late in generation. Fixed search rules or excessive parallel sampling can therefore allocate computation poorly.

The method is a training-free controller for multi-path decoding in mixture-of-experts models. It uses lightweight path statistics to expand or reduce the hypothesis pool within a fixed budget. A token-level refinement mechanism supports exploitation during generation without resampling entire paths. A separate answer-aggregation rule considers length and confidence, addressing the gap between generating a correct answer somewhere and selecting it reliably.

Across four mixture-of-experts models and diverse benchmarks, HyPER reports improvements of 8–10% over prior methods while reducing token consumption by 25–40%. Its reported accuracy–compute frontier supports adapting computational allocation throughout reasoning and treating final answer selection as a distinct part of that allocation.
icml-2026-hyper-bridging-exploration-and.tldr: HyPER dynamically allocates a fixed reasoning budget across exploring, refining, and selecting hypothesis paths in mixture-of-experts language models.

paragraphs: Online construction of vectorized high-definition maps is an important component of autonomous driving. Many leading methods treat map construction as detecting separate instances using learned object queries. The paper argues that this encourages a local perspective, leaving the map’s overall structure insufficiently represented in the queries used to construct it.

MapGR introduces two complementary modules. Global Representation Learning uses a holistic segmentation task to encourage the collection of queries to align with the complete map. Global Representation Guidance then supplies individual queries with explicit global context to help optimize them. One module develops a shared view of the map, while the other makes that view available to each local prediction.

Evaluations on nuScenes and Argoverse2 report substantial gains in mean Average Precision over leading baselines. These results support the value of combining instance-level detection with map-wide representation learning. The contribution is a mechanism for making queries reflect both their individual targets and the broader spatial structure they collectively describe.
icml-2026-learning-global-representation.tldr: MapGR improves vectorized map construction by teaching object queries to learn and use global map context.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization chooses actions over successive rounds and evaluates performance against a reference sequence of decisions. Dynamic regret allows that reference to change over time. This paper studies an unconstrained setting where changing the learner’s own decisions also incurs a movement cost, and the coefficient of that cost may vary arbitrarily between rounds.

The proposed algorithm provides a comparator-adaptive regret bound scaling, up to logarithmic factors, with the square root of (M² + M P_T) times (T + the sum of movement-cost coefficients). Here, M describes the largest reference-decision norm and P_T measures how far the reference sequence moves. When movement costs vanish, the result recovers optimal adaptive rates for static and dynamic regret.

The authors also translate delayed-feedback problems and problems with time-varying memory into this movement-cost framework. A new reduction handles delayed feedback specifically. The linear appearance of accumulated movement costs inside the bound is crucial to obtaining optimal comparator-adaptive dynamic-regret guarantees in both applications, connecting several online-learning settings through one analysis.
icml-2026-parameter-free-dynamic-regret-.tldr: A new adaptive regret bound handles arbitrarily varying movement costs and yields guarantees for online learning with delays or changing memory.

paragraphs: Training large language models requires substantial memory and computation, alongside an optimization method that remains stable. POET addresses stability by updating weight matrices through orthogonal equivalence transformations that preserve their spectrum. However, its original implementation uses intensive matrix multiplication, creating memory and computational overhead that restricts its practical scalability.

POET-X retains this transformation-based training approach while reducing the cost of carrying it out. The paper presents it as a scalable variant that preserves POET’s generalization and stability benefits while improving throughput and memory efficiency. The contribution therefore concerns making an existing structured optimization framework more practical for larger models, without giving up the properties that motivated that framework.

In the reported experiments, POET-X makes it possible to pretrain billion-parameter language models on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Standard optimizers such as AdamW run out of memory under the same settings. This comparison demonstrates a concrete change in training feasibility within the tested configuration, beyond an improvement in optimization efficiency alone.
icml-2026-poet-x-memory-efficient-llm-tr.tldr: POET-X reduces the overhead of orthogonal-transformation training, enabling billion-parameter language-model pretraining on one H100 in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Model editing aims to correct a pretrained model’s mistakes while preserving unrelated behavior. For vision–language models, reasoning-heavy questions introduce a further challenge: a correction may depend on an explanation of how to interpret an image. ReasonEdit introduces an editing setup in which users supply that reasoning, giving the editor more information than an answer correction alone.

The system continually stores human reasoning in a codebook. At inference time, it retrieves relevant facts using a topology-balanced multimodal embedding method inspired by network science. This connects the stored explanations to the current visual question, so the model can draw on applicable reasoning when answering. Selective retrieval is central to making accumulated edits useful across different questions.

Experiments evaluate four vision–language models on multiple visual question-answering datasets containing rationales. ReasonEdit achieves leading editing performance, and the results show that incorporating human reasoning substantially improves edit generalization. This suggests that explanations can help corrections apply beyond the particular example that originally prompted an edit.
icml-2026-reasonedit-editing-visionlangu.tldr: ReasonEdit stores and retrieves human explanations to make vision–language model corrections generalize better across reasoning-heavy visual questions.

paragraphs: Larger models and more training data are often expected to improve time-series forecasting. This paper tests that expectation for language models adapted to forecasting and foundation models trained for time series. Experiments across two model families, four sizes from 100 million to 1.7 billion parameters, and datasets containing up to six billion observations find that larger models do not always perform better.

Analysis of internal representations identifies few-layer dominance: a small subset of layers contributes most of the useful function, while many others are redundant, underused, or can distract training. The authors develop a method that automatically identifies and retains the dominant layers, using the diagnosis to guide model reduction.

In their models, retaining 21% of parameters delivers up to 12% better accuracy and a 2.7-fold inference speedup. Further evaluation on eight leading models finds that keeping fewer than 30% of layers improves accuracy on over 95% of tested tasks. These results show that selective reduction can improve both efficiency and accuracy within the evaluated forecasting models.
icml-2026-revealing-scaling-paradox-in-l.tldr: The paper finds that a few layers dominate many time-series models and shows that retaining them can improve accuracy while reducing inference cost.

paragraphs: A watermarking system must balance how much information it embeds, how well that information survives distortion, and how little it changes the visible image. Deep learning has improved resistance to real-world noise, but its watermarking performance deteriorates as message size grows. Coding-based methods avoid that payload-dimension problem, although they are less robust to real-world noise.

OrthoMark separates these responsibilities. A learned feature extractor first produces a representation designed to remain stable under distortion. Coding-based methods then encode and decode the message in that feature space. This assigns robustness learning to the neural component and message representation to the coding component, combining the strengths identified in the two approaches.

Extensive experiments report a substantially improved balance between visual quality, robustness, and capacity compared with earlier deep watermarking methods. The gains are especially large for high-capacity messages. These results support separating robust feature extraction from message encoding as an effective way to address the payload-scaling problem in learning-based watermarking.
icml-2026-revisiting-coding-based-approa.tldr: OrthoMark combines learned distortion-resistant features with coding-based message embedding to improve watermarking, especially at high payload capacity.

paragraphs: Derivative-free optimization must infer useful information from function evaluations without directly accessing derivatives. Estimating curvature through a Hessian matrix, or using its inverse, is especially difficult in high dimensions because randomized estimates can have high variance. This paper develops a common framework for understanding and improving several such estimators.

The framework connects general zeroth-order Hessian estimators to the Hessian of a smoothed, single-step policy-optimization objective. Within this connection, classical estimators correspond to different baseline choices. The resulting ZoVH suite estimates the full Hessian, its regularized inverse, and a bias-corrected inverse-Hessian–gradient product. It uses a uniquely optimal variance-minimizing baseline and reuses historical function queries to improve sample efficiency without increasing query costs.

The analysis establishes unbiasedness for the Hessian estimator, variance optimality for the baseline, error bounds across the suite, and convergence guarantees for the resulting curvature-aware algorithm. Experiments report improved estimation accuracy and convergence. The contribution combines a unifying theoretical interpretation with practical mechanisms for reducing noise in curvature estimates.
icml-2026-revisiting-zeroth-order-hessia.tldr: ZoVH uses a policy-optimization interpretation, an optimal baseline, and reused function queries to improve derivative-free curvature estimation.

paragraphs: Patch-based forecasting divides a time series into segments to represent temporal patterns. Using every segment can be problematic when some contain missing values, anomalies, noise, or distribution shifts. SEER addresses this by learning both stronger patch representations and a way to identify and replace patches that would otherwise harm prediction.

Its Augmented Embedding Module uses a mixture-of-experts architecture to improve individual patch representations. A channel-adaptive mechanism also builds tokens representing the broader series. The Learnable Patch Replacement Module then filters harmful patch tokens and replaces the identified low-quality patches with global series-level information. Causal attention further refines these representations as part of the prediction process.

The reported experiments show state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The central contribution is an adaptive treatment of input quality: the model can draw on broader series information where local segments are unreliable. Combining representation enhancement with learned replacement provides a concrete mechanism for making patch-based forecasts more robust to imperfect collected data.
icml-2026-seer-transformer-based-robust-.tldr: SEER improves time-series forecasting by enhancing patch representations and replacing harmful patches with learned global series information.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer an energy-efficient approach to three-dimensional perception, but weak pretraining and heavy inference components have limited their generalization and multimodal reasoning. SVL develops vision–language pretraining that connects 3D, image, and text information while preserving spike-based processing throughout the system.

Multi-scale Triple Alignment uses a label-free contrastive objective to align the three modalities. Re-parameterizable Vision–Language Integration converts text embeddings computed offline into lightweight weights, removing the need for a text encoder during inference. The paper also introduces Spike-driven PointFormer, whose 3D self-attention expresses interactions through sparse additions to support faster, more efficient training.

Experiments report 85.4% top-1 accuracy for zero-shot 3D classification and improvements over previous spiking models in classification, action recognition, detection, and segmentation. SVL also enables open-world 3D question answering and sometimes outperforms conventional artificial neural networks. These results support combining multimodal pretraining with an efficient spike-driven architecture to broaden the range of tasks that spiking networks can handle.
icml-2026-svl-empowering-spiking-neural-.tldr: SVL aligns 3D, image, and text representations to give efficient spiking networks zero-shot recognition and open-world question-answering capabilities.

paragraphs: Observational data often represent a selected portion of a population. A biobank, for example, may attract volunteers who are healthier and more affluent than the people it is intended to represent. Consequently, an average treatment effect estimated from participants may differ substantially from the effect in the wider population. This paper asks when that population effect can be identified despite selection.

The authors provide necessary and sufficient conditions for identifying the average treatment effect within their framework. Their analysis uses assumptions on probability classes to characterize both propensity scores and selection probabilities. These assumptions are weaker than those required by existing general identification frameworks, allowing the results to cover a broader set of circumstances.

The findings extend existing graphical criteria for causal identification under selection bias. Their importance lies in clarifying both when recovery is possible and when the identification conditions are not satisfied. The contribution is therefore a sharper theoretical characterization of what selected observational data can establish about population-level causal effects under the stated assumptions.
icml-2026-towards-a-holistic-understandi.tldr: The paper characterizes when population average treatment effects are identifiable under selection bias using weaker assumptions than existing general frameworks.

paragraphs: Answering questions about long videos requires finding scattered evidence among large amounts of irrelevant content. VideoSEAL identifies a failure that answer accuracy alone can miss: an agent may answer correctly even though the frames it retrieved or inspected do not support its answer. The paper measures this mismatch through temporal and semantic groundedness.

The analysis finds that crowded shared context during inference and rewards based only on final outcomes during training can increase misalignment. VideoSEAL responds by separating long-horizon planning from authority to answer. A planner directs the search, while an inspector verifies visual evidence; final answering is gated on pixel-level verification. This makes evidence checking a structural part of the workflow.

Across four long-video benchmarks, the framework improves accuracy and evidence alignment, reaching 55.1% on LVBench and 62.0% on LongVideoBench. It also produces interpretable search trajectories, benefits consistently from larger search budgets, and allows multimodal-model upgrades without retraining the planner. These results connect stronger grounding with useful flexibility in search and model selection.
icml-2026-videoseal-mitigating-evidence-.tldr: VideoSEAL separates video-search planning from answer authority and requires visual verification to improve both accuracy and evidence alignment.

paragraphs: Learning directly on neuromorphic devices could let spiking neural networks adapt after deployment. Zeroth-order optimization is attractive for this purpose because it learns through forward evaluations, reducing the hardware complexity associated with backward computation. However, the paper shows that applying such methods to spiking networks is difficult because their step-like activations amplify variance.

The proposed Subspace-based Zeroth-Order method, SZO, responds by restricting learning to a low-dimensional subspace. It draws on the observed low-dimensional structure of the network’s optimization trajectory, concentrating perturbation-based updates within that space. This addresses the variance problem while retaining a forward-only learning procedure suitable for the paper’s motivation of on-chip adaptation.

The authors evaluate training from scratch, continual training, and unsupervised adaptation. SZO reaches accuracy comparable to first-order methods and learns faster than full-space backpropagation in the reported experiments. These findings show that selecting a suitable optimization subspace can substantially improve forward-only training, bringing its performance close to first-order learning across the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-zeroth-order-forward-only-snn-.tldr: SZO trains spiking networks with forward-only updates in a low-dimensional subspace, approaching first-order accuracy while improving learning speed.
